title: Inaccessible rocky cliffs: An optimized method for plant data collection in extreme environments
author: Alfaro-Saiz, Granda, et al.

steps.title: Select cliffs and photograph walls
steps.instruction: Locate the target cliff populations, choose the specific cliffs to monitor, and take a photograph of each wall ensuring maximum perpendicularity; if a cliff is very wide, take several photos at regular distances.

steps.title: Scale images and create grid
steps.instruction: Import each photograph into GIS software, adjust the image dimensions so they correspond to the real distances (following Goñi et al.), overlay a 10 × 10 m grid, assign a unique identification code to every grid‑cell, and delete edge cells that contain only a very small percentage of rock (as illustrated in Fig. 1). The example wall area is approximately 1470 m².

steps.title: Count visual units with telescope
steps.instruction: From a distance of 400 m, use a 20× terrestrial telescope to count the number of observable individuals (“visual units”) in each grid‑cell; the count may be restricted to mature individuals if required.

steps.title: Determine correction factor (CF)
steps.instruction: Select 30–40 easily delimited accessible areas; for each area perform two counts – one with the 20× lens used for the main survey and another with a higher‑magnification 60× lens; compute the ratio 20×/60× (or real individuals/visual units) for each area, repeat the procedure for every observer and sampling year, normalize the ratios to a normal distribution, calculate the mean ratio, and multiply this mean by the total visual units recorded for each grid‑cell to obtain corrected individual numbers.

steps.title: Aggregate cell counts
steps.instruction: Sum the corrected individual numbers from all grid‑cells to obtain the total population estimate for the entire cliff face (full‑face data collection is recommended).

steps.title: Import data into R
steps.instruction: Open R, install and load the packages MASS, fitdistrplus, readxl, dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2.

steps.title: Fit candidate distributions
steps.instruction: Using the fitdistrplus functions, fit Geometric, Poisson, and Negative Binomial distributions to the aggregated count data and obtain observed and theoretical frequencies for each model.

steps.title: Assess goodness‑of‑fit
steps.instruction: Perform graphical comparisons and a chi‑square (χ²) test for each fitted distribution; null hypothesis H₀: observed frequencies do not differ significantly from expected frequencies; reject H₀ if p‑value < 0.05.

steps.title: Select best model via criteria
steps.instruction: Calculate Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) for each distribution and choose the model with the lowest AIC/BIC as the best fit.

steps.title: Generate diagnostic plots
steps.instruction: Create a Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) plot, a PP plot, and a QQ plot for the selected best‑fit model to visually evaluate the fit.

steps.title: Determine minimum sample size
steps.instruction: Using the parameters of the best‑fit distribution, generate random subsets of the full data by sampling grid‑cells at decreasing percentages: start at 90 % and reduce by 5 % increments down to 5 %; for each subset estimate the population size and compute confidence intervals.

steps.title: Compute confidence intervals
steps.instruction: For each sampled subset calculate confidence intervals (CI) by two methods: (i) Maximum Likelihood (ML) approximation of the normal log‑transformed variable, and (ii) Simple Bootstrap (SB) where the subset is resampled with replacement 10 000 times; repeat the entire bootstrap procedure 25 times for each sampling level.

steps.title: Visualize results and choose effort
steps.instruction: Plot box‑and‑whisker diagrams showing CI (mean, max, min) and estimated population for the 25 repetitions at each sampling percentage; compare ML and SB CI widths and select the sampling percentage that yields the smallest error bar (e.g., 55 % in the example) as the minimum effort; adopt the method (ML or SB) that provides the lowest CI for final reporting.
